title: Association between late-pregnancy household food insecurity and birth weight: Evidence from Propensity Score Matching
content:
by Mohamedawel Mohamedniguss Ebrahim, Nobel Aklilu Abay, Netsanet Mezgebe Aregawi

Background

Food insecurity, a situation characterized by the absence or limited access to sufficient quality and quantity of food to meet dietary needs, exposes mothers to adverse pregnancy outcomes such as birth defects and low birth weight. Nevertheless, despite the massive burden of food insecurity among pregnant and lactating women residing in resource-limited and war-affected settings like Tigray, Northern Ethiopia, there is a scarcity of evidence on the effect of food insecurity on pregnancy outcomes, more specifically, birthweight. Therefore, the aim of this study was to assess the association between late-pregnancy household food insecurity and birthweight using propensity score matching.

Method

A facility-based cross-sectional study was conducted at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Mekelle, Tigray Region, Northern Ethiopia, from December 2024 to March 2025. The study included 286 mother–newborn pairs recruited using systematic random sampling. Data were collected by trained midwives using a structured questionnaire and checklist. Food security status was assessed using the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale. Data were analyzed in STATA version 19. Propensity score matching (PSM) was used to assess the effect of household food insecurity on birth weight. Results of PSM are reported using the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) and the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATET). In addition, crude comparisons of mean differences were made using either the Independent-Samples T-Test or One-Way ANOVA. Statistical significance was declared at p < 0.05. In addition, subgroup, sensitivity, and robust multiple linear regression analyses methods are used to assess effect robustness and detect a dose-response relationship.

Result

The mean age of the mothers was 28.7 years (SD = 3.9). Of the total participants, 177 (61.9%) were food-secure, while the remaining 109 (38.1%) were food-insecure. Among the food-insecure group, 49 (17.1%) experienced mild food insecurity, 40 (14.0%) moderate food insecurity, and 20 (7.0%) severe food insecurity. The magnitude of low birthweight (LBW) among food-insecure mothers was 48.6%, compared to 11.3% among food-secure mothers. Overall, the prevalence of LBW was 25.5%. On average, the birthweight of newborns born to food-insecure mothers was 204 grams lower (ATE = –204.0, 95% CI: –289.3 to –118.7, p < 0.001) than that of newborns born to food-secure mothers. Furthermore, the birthweight of newborns born to food-insecure mothers was 218 grams lower compared to the birthweight they would have had if their mothers had been food secure (ATET = –218.3, 95% CI: –411.2 to –25.3, p = 0.027).

Conclusions

Late-pregnancy maternal food insecurity was significantly associated with decreased neonatal birthweight and an increase in the magnitude of LBW. Hence, addressing maternal food access could substantially decrease the burden of LBW and its related complications. During antenatal care, emphasis should be placed on assessing a pregnant woman’s nutritional and food security statuses, and on integrating social and behavioral nutrition interventions to promote food security. In addition, a focus should be given to nutrition education before and during pregnancy. Policymakers should also ensure food security and improve nutritional conditions by empowering women.
